interest: Documents US fears Japanese economic penetration of the Philippines, centered on Davao, could turn it into 'another Korea or Manchukuo'.
overview: This State Department file (decimal file 894.20211B/14, classified under Japanese military activities, espionage, and propaganda in the Philippine Islands) centers on an extensive October 1937 War Department study prepared by Brigadier General Charles Burnett, Chief of the Bureau of Insular Affairs, entitled 'Japanese Penetration of the Philippine Islands', transmitted by Adviser on International Economic Affairs Herbert Feis to Under Secretary of State Sumner Welles in November 1937. Burnett's memorandum provides a comprehensive military and economic intelligence assessment of Japanese demographic, commercial, and industrial inroads in the Commonwealth of the Philippines, focusing on the concentration of Japanese settlers in Davao, Mindanao, their dominance of the abacá (hemp) and fishing industries, commercial retail competition against Chinese and Filipino merchants, and Japan's demand for vital strategic minerals such as iron ore and chromite. Burnett argues that the scheduled elimination of U.S. tariff preferences upon Philippine independence would inevitably collapse the Philippine export economy and leave the islands entirely dependent upon, and politically vulnerable to, the Japanese Empire. The file also includes a February 1936 memorandum from Stanley K. Hornbeck of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs regarding coordination with Ernest Gruening and Edward C. Carter, alongside a New York Times clipping concerning allegations of pro-Japanese bias in an Institute of Pacific Relations school textbook in Hawaii.

subfiles.about: Comprehensive War Department intelligence report analyzing Japan's economic, commercial, demographic, and political penetration of the Philippine Islands and the strategic outlook following independence.
subfiles.from: Charles Burnett (Brigadier General, U.S. Army; Chief of Bureau of Insular Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Brigadier General Charles Burnett examines the nature and trajectory of Japanese expansionism in the Far East and its specific ramifications for the Philippine Islands before and after independence. The report analyzes the growing Japanese population centered in Davao, Mindanao, where Japanese settlers dominate abacá (hemp) cultivation, control over 100,000 acres, and run deep-sea commercial fishing operations that have supplanted native enterprise. Burnett details Japan's capture of Philippine retail trade following anti-Japanese boycotts by Chinese merchants, as well as Japan's strategic interest in Philippine raw materials including iron ore, chromite, lumber, and potential cotton crops. He concludes that terminating U.S. free trade and preferential tariffs will devastate major Philippine export industries, inevitably forcing an independent Philippines into total economic dependency and potential political subjugation by Japan.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Brigadier General Charles Burnett on Japanese Penetration of the Philippine Islands
subfiles.to: Herbert Feis (Adviser on International Economic Affairs, Department of State)

subfiles.about: Newspaper report on the official rejection by Hawaii school officials of charges alleging pro-Japanese bias in an Institute of Pacific Relations textbook.

subfiles.summary: NYT Honolulu dispatch: Oscar Shepard refutes V. S. McClatchy's claim that Ruth Pratt's IPR textbook on Japan, used experimentally in few Hawaii schools, spread pro-Japanese propaganda.
